| 2026-09-15 | uc3/P5 | the audit chain has no anchor outside the database, so it is tamper-evident but not non-repudiable (ADR 0011) | an unkeyed sha256 chain can be recomputed by anyone who can edit the rows: the implementation's own benchmark walks and hashes 10,003 rows in 0.46 s, so an actor with `UPDATE` on `analysis_runs`/`flags`/`dispositions` (superuser, table owner, a restored snapshot) can rewrite the tail, re-chain it and leave `chain_verify` reporting `ok`. The local anchor (head hash + row count, `0009_uc3_chain_anchor`) adds a second row that must also be rewritten, but it sits in the same database under the same privilege and is recomputed with the same unkeyed hash, so it is a cross-check, not a trust root. Closing this needs a trust root outside the database, which this repository cannot provide: a signing key the database hosts cannot reach (Key Vault), or a WORM bucket with a retention lock, or an external notary. Nothing in P5 was narrowed to avoid it -- the chain, the role and the nightly verify are all built and tested | `program/P10-azure-deploy`: provision the Key Vault signing key or the immutable-storage container, publish a daily `(table, head_hash, row_count, timestamp)` record to it, extend `chain_verify` to compare the walked head against that external record, and hold backup credentials separately from the production role. Until then `uc3/P7`'s control mapping must carry the weaker claim |  |
| 2026-09-15 | uc3/P5 | `uc3_app` is not the role the application connects as, so the least-privilege control is proven but not yet on the path production traffic takes | the role is created, constrained to `select, insert` on the three chained tables and proven by `test_the_app_role_cannot_update_or_delete_the_audit_tables` (Postgres logged four denials in the same CI run), but nothing in this repository sets the runtime DSN: the app still connects as the migration/owner role, which carries `UPDATE`/`DELETE` implicitly and can re-grant them to itself. There is no environment to wire it in -- no deployed database, no provisioned login role, no secret store -- and inventing one in `.env.example` would read as configured when it is not. `0008_uc3_audit_role.py` records the precondition in its docstring: the app's login role must not own the audit tables and must hold no direct grants on them beyond its membership of `uc3_app` | `program/P10-azure-deploy`: provision a login role that is a member of `uc3_app` and owns nothing in `public`, run migrations as a separate owner role, point the application's DSN at the former, and add a startup assertion that an `UPDATE` on a chained table is refused so a misconfigured deployment fails loudly rather than silently losing the control |  |
| 2026-09-15 | uc3/P5 | the chain hashes the Python object the application built, not the JSON bytes Postgres stores, so a JSONB round-trip difference in `analysis_runs.output` could produce a permanent, unrepairable false break | `append` hashes `canonical_json(row_payload(row))` before the INSERT; `verify_chain` re-hashes the row as psycopg reads it back, after Postgres has parsed and re-rendered the JSONB. The two are equal only while the round-trip is exact, and JSONB does not promise that: numbers are reparsed as `numeric` and re-rendered (exponent forms and some float spellings do not survive), and non-string mapping keys come back as strings, which changes their `sort_keys` order (`1, 2, 10` becomes `"1", "10", "2"`) and therefore the canonical bytes. A row that diverges this way is reported as "row_hash does not match the row content: the row was edited" forever, and cannot be repaired: the tables are append-only by design and by grant, so there is no UPDATE available to rewrite the stored hash. Mitigation actually in place, which is why this is a latent risk and not a live defect: the only JSONB column on a chained table is `output`, whose payloads are model-generated JSON with string keys, and the detector and eval paths construct no `Decimal` and no non-string keys. No such break has been observed in the 10 pure and 7 integration tests or in the 10k-row benchmark | hash the serialized JSON text that is actually inserted rather than the Python object -- serialize `output` once with `canonical_json`, bind that text, and have `verify_chain` read the stored text back (`output::text`) and hash the same bytes -- so the hash describes what the database holds. It is a change to the hashing input, so it must land as a new chain rather than a rehash of existing rows, or be done before any chain carries data that matters; a regression test that round-trips awkward payloads (floats in exponent form, integer keys, Decimals) through Postgres and re-verifies belongs with it |  |
